stem: The famous bronze figure of the 'Dancing Girl' belongs to the __________ civilisation.
solution: The Dancing Girl is a Harappan bronze sculpture from Mohenjodaro.

stem: The 'Dancing Girl' of Mohenjodaro was made using the __________ technique.
solution: The Dancing Girl was cast in bronze by the lost-wax (cire perdue) technique.

stem: The stone sculpture of the 'Bearded Priest-King' was found at __________.
solution: The steatite 'Priest-King' figure was found at Mohenjodaro.

stem: The 'Priest-King' figure of the Indus Valley is carved from __________.
solution: The Priest-King is carved from steatite (soapstone).

stem: The shawl of the Priest-King figure is decorated with a __________ motif.
solution: The shawl is decorated with a trefoil (three-leaf) pattern.

stem: The most characteristic and numerous art objects of the Indus Valley are the __________.
solution: Seals, mostly of steatite, are the most typical and numerous Harappan artefacts.

stem: Most Indus Valley seals were made of __________.
solution: Most Harappan seals were made of steatite (soapstone).

stem: The most famous Indus seal, showing a figure surrounded by animals, is called the __________ seal.
solution: The Pashupati seal shows a seated figure surrounded by animals.

stem: The Pashupati seal depicts a seated figure surrounded by an elephant, a tiger, a rhinoceros and a __________.
solution: The Pashupati seal shows an elephant, tiger, rhinoceros and buffalo, with deer beneath the seat.

stem: The animal most frequently depicted on Indus Valley seals is the __________.
solution: The 'unicorn' (a one-horned bull) is the most common animal on Harappan seals.

stem: The purpose of the Indus seals was most likely __________.
solution: Seals were mainly used in trade to mark ownership and identify goods.

stem: The Indus Valley script on the seals is written __________.
options: from right to left (boustrophedon in some cases)
solution: The undeciphered Indus script generally runs right to left.

stem: Terracotta figures of the Indus Valley were made of __________.
solution: Terracotta figurines were made of fire-baked clay.

stem: The most important terracotta figures of the Indus Valley are those of the __________.
solution: Terracotta 'Mother Goddess' figures are the most notable of Harappan clay art.

stem: A famous red sandstone torso, showing advanced modelling, was found at __________.
solution: The red sandstone male torso was found at Harappa.

stem: The Harappan red sandstone torso is remarkable for its __________.
options: realistic modelling of the human body
solution: The torso shows a highly realistic, sensitive modelling of the human body.

stem: The Indus Valley people were skilled in making ornaments from __________.
options: gold, silver, ivory and precious stones
solution: Harappans made jewellery from gold, silver, ivory, copper and semi-precious stones.

stem: The town of Chanhudaro was an important centre for the manufacture of __________.
solution: Chanhudaro was a specialised centre for bead-making.

stem: The Harappan pottery was mostly __________ ware.
solution: Harappan pottery is chiefly red ware painted with black designs.

stem: The designs on Harappan painted pottery include __________.
options: intersecting circles, trees, birds and geometric motifs
solution: Pottery is decorated with intersecting circles, trees, animals, birds and geometric patterns.

stem: The bronze casting of the Indus Valley shows that Harappans knew the technique of __________.
options: mixing copper with tin (bronze) and lost-wax casting
solution: Harappans made bronze (copper + tin) and used lost-wax casting.

stem: The 'Dancing Girl' bronze is shown in a pose that is __________.
options: confident and relaxed, with one hand on the hip
solution: The Dancing Girl stands in a confident, relaxed pose with a hand on the hip.

stem: The bronze figures found at Mohenjodaro and other Harappan sites are cast using the technique in which a wax model is __________.
options: covered in clay and melted out, then filled with molten metal
solution: In lost-wax casting, the wax model is covered with clay, melted out, and replaced with molten metal.

stem: Indus Valley seals were often engraved with the figure on the __________.
solution: Seal designs were engraved in intaglio (sunken relief) on the front face.

stem: The Indus Valley art is notable for its __________ despite the small size of most objects.
options: high level of craftsmanship and realism
solution: Harappan art shows remarkable craftsmanship and realism in small objects.

stem: Many terracotta toys such as carts and animals with movable heads show that the Harappans made objects for __________.
solution: Terracotta toys indicate objects made for children's play and everyday use.

stem: The Indus civilisation flourished around __________.
solution: The mature Harappan phase flourished around 2500 BCE.

stem: Which of the following was NOT commonly produced by Indus Valley artisans?
solution: The Harappans did not build large stone temples; they made seals, terracotta and bronze objects.

stem: The steatite used for seals was chosen because it is __________.
options: soft and easy to carve, then hardened by heating
solution: Steatite is soft and easy to carve, and can be hardened by heating after engraving.

stem: The Harappan beads were made from materials such as carnelian, agate, and __________.
solution: Beads were made of carnelian, agate, jasper, steatite, gold and other materials.

stem: A distinctive type of carnelian bead of the Indus Valley was decorated with white designs using a technique called __________.
solution: Etched (bleached) carnelian beads with white designs were a Harappan speciality.

stem: The Indus Valley art forms us that the civilisation valued __________.
solution: Harappan art reflects a society valuing trade, fine craft and aesthetics.

stem: The Priest-King figure has half-closed eyes, suggesting a __________ expression.
solution: The half-closed eyes give the Priest-King a meditative expression.

stem: The technique of making figures by pinching and joining pieces of clay is seen in Harappan __________.
solution: Terracotta figurines were made by hand-modelling and joining clay pieces.

stem: The realism in the Harappan bronze and stone figures indicates a __________ tradition of sculpture.
solution: The figures reflect a mature, sophisticated sculptural tradition.

stem: Harappan seals often carry, along with the animal, a short line of __________.
solution: Seals combine an animal figure with a short line of the pictographic Indus script.

stem: The Indus artisans achieved fine detail in seals despite their __________.
solution: Despite being small, the seals show finely detailed and precise engraving.

stem: The Mother Goddess terracotta figures usually have elaborate __________.
solution: Mother Goddess figures are shown with elaborate head-dresses and jewellery.

stem: The Harappan civilisation is also called the __________ civilisation.
solution: The Harappan civilisation is also known as the Indus Valley civilisation.

stem: Which material was used for the famous 'Dancing Girl'?
solution: The Dancing Girl is a bronze sculpture.

stem: The Harappan seals were probably also used as __________.
solution: Besides trade, seals may also have been used as amulets.

stem: The most common shape of the Indus Valley seal is __________.
options: square with a perforated boss at the back
solution: Most seals are square with a small perforated knob (boss) at the back for handling.

stem: The presence of a small perforated boss on the back of a seal suggests it could be __________.
options: worn or hung with a cord
solution: The perforated boss allowed the seal to be worn or carried on a cord.

stem: The theme of the Pashupati seal is often interpreted as an early form of __________.
solution: The Pashupati (yogic) figure is often seen as a possible proto-Shiva.

stem: Indus Valley art shows that the people had knowledge of __________.
solution: Their bronze work shows advanced knowledge of metallurgy and casting.

stem: The red sandstone torso from Harappa and the grey stone dancing figure show mastery over __________.
options: depicting the human body in movement
solution: These sculptures show mastery in depicting the human body, including movement.

stem: The Harappan artisans made a wide variety of __________ used in weaving and stitching.
solution: Tools like spindle whorls and needles show Harappan textile activity.

stem: The overall impression given by Indus Valley art is one of __________.
solution: Indus art conveys refinement, realism and high craftsmanship in small objects.

stem: The seals of the Indus Valley are an important source for studying its __________.
solution: Seals are key evidence for Harappan trade, religion and the undeciphered script.

stem: The Indus Valley civilisation belongs to the __________ Age.
solution: The Harappan civilisation is a Bronze Age civilisation.
